templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: Calculate the number of moles in {m} g of {name} (molar mass = {M} g mol⁻¹), and the number of formula units it contains. Take N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

solutionChain.statement: mass = {m} g, molar mass = {M} g mol⁻¹, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹
solutionChain.justification: Molar mass carries the unit g mol⁻¹. It is NOT the same thing as relative molecular mass, which has no unit.
The mole is the SI amount of substance: dividing grams by grams-per-mole leaves moles.
One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles, whatever the substance is.

misconceptions.feedback: You inverted the ratio. Check the units: g mol⁻¹ ÷ g gives mol⁻¹, not mol. Writing the unit on every line catches this before the marks go.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Both numbers are 'masses', so the order feels arbitrary when you are moving fast.

misconceptions.statement: Multiplied the mass directly by Avogadro's number.
misconceptions.feedback: N_A converts MOLES to particles, not grams to particles. You need n = m/M first — that is the bridge between the lab and the particles.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Avogadro's number is the only 'particle' number in the question, so it looks like the one multiplication you need.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: In the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, {mN} g of nitrogen is mixed with {mH} g of hydrogen. Molar masses: N₂ = 28 g mol⁻¹, H₂ = 2 g mol⁻¹, NH₃ = 17 g mol⁻¹. Identify the limiting reagent and calculate the maximum mass of ammonia formed.

solutionChain.statement: Balanced equation: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. m(N₂) = {mN} g, m(H₂) = {mH} g
solutionChain.justification: Balance first, always. Mole ratios read off an unbalanced equation are worth nothing.
Convert every mass to moles before comparing anything. Masses cannot be compared across different substances.
Same conversion for the second reactant.

solutionChain.statement: Divide each by its coefficient: N₂ → n/1, H₂ → n/3. The smaller value is the limiting reagent.
solutionChain.justification: The limiting reagent is the one with the smallest moles-÷-coefficient, NOT the smallest mass.
Two moles of ammonia come from each unit of the limiting quantity; convert back to grams at the very end.

misconceptions.statement: Took the reagent with the smaller MASS as limiting.
misconceptions.feedback: Limiting is decided by moles ÷ coefficient, never by mass. {mH} g of H₂ is {mH/2} mol; {mN} g of N₂ is {mN/28} mol — the smaller mass is often the larger amount of substance.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: 'Less of it, so it runs out first' is true for identical particles — and hydrogen molecules are 14 times lighter than nitrogen ones.

misconceptions.statement: Compared moles without dividing by the coefficients.
misconceptions.feedback: You compared n(N₂) with n(H₂) directly. The equation needs THREE H₂ for every one N₂, so hydrogen must be divided by 3 before the comparison.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Once both are in moles it feels like the units are finally comparable — but the stoichiometry has not been applied yet.

misconceptions.statement: Applied the mole ratio to grams.
misconceptions.feedback: The 1 : 3 : 2 ratio applies to MOLES only. Applying it to grams is the single most common stoichiometry error in Nepal — it even shows up in teaching notes.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The coefficients sit right next to the formulas, and the masses are the numbers you were given, so they get combined.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: {m} g of a solute of molar mass {M} g mol⁻¹ is dissolved in water and made up to {V} cm³ of solution. Calculate the molarity of the solution.

solutionChain.statement: m = {m} g, M = {M} g mol⁻¹, V = {V} cm³ = {V}/1000 dm³
solutionChain.justification: Molarity is per cubic decimetre (litre). Convert the volume first — cm³ into a molarity calculation is a 1000× error.
Amount of solute in moles.
Molarity is moles of solute per dm³ of SOLUTION, not per dm³ of solvent.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a concentration in g dm⁻³, not a molarity. Molarity always counts particles, so the mass has to become moles first.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Both are called 'concentration' in everyday speech, and both go up when you add more solid.

misconceptions.feedback: Your answer is 1000 times too small. Molarity is mol dm⁻³, so {V} cm³ has to become {V/1000} dm³.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The question hands you cm³, so cm³ feels like the working unit.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: A compound has molar mass {M} g mol⁻¹ and each mole contains {n} mol of oxygen atoms (A_r of O = 16). Calculate the percentage of oxygen by mass in the compound.

solutionChain.statement: Molar mass = {M} g mol⁻¹; oxygen contributes {n} × 16 g mol⁻¹
solutionChain.justification: Relative atomic mass (16) has no unit; molar mass (16 g mol⁻¹) does. Keep the two apart in your working.
Multiply the number of oxygen atoms per formula unit by the atomic mass of oxygen.
A percentage by mass is always part-mass over whole-mass.

misconceptions.statement: Used the number of oxygen atoms instead of their mass.
misconceptions.feedback: Percentage BY MASS needs the mass of oxygen, which is {n} × 16 = {n*16} g mol⁻¹, not the count {n}.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: 'Percentage of oxygen' sounds like a count of atoms, and the atom count is the number in front of you.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.problemTypeLabel: Molar volume of a gas at STP
templates.template: Calculate the volume occupied at STP by {m} g of a gas of molar mass {M} g mol⁻¹. Take the molar volume at STP as 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹.

solutionChain.statement: m = {m} g, M = {M} g mol⁻¹, V_m = 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹ at STP
solutionChain.justification: 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹ applies to GASES at STP only — never to a solid, a liquid, or a gas at some other temperature and pressure.
Convert to moles first; the molar volume is per mole.
Avogadro's law: equal amounts of any gas occupy equal volumes at the same temperature and pressure.

misconceptions.feedback: 22.4 dm³ is the volume of one MOLE, not of one gram. Convert to moles first: n = {m}/{M} = {m/M} mol.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: 22.4 is the only volume number in the question, so it looks like a straight conversion factor.

misconceptions.feedback: More gas means more volume, so n and V must multiply. Sanity-check the direction before you press equals.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The previous step was a division, and the hand keeps going.

templates.subject: Chemistry
templates.template: {n} mol of an ideal gas occupies a container of volume {V} dm³ at a temperature of {T} °C. Taking R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, calculate the pressure of the gas in pascals.

solutionChain.statement: n = {n} mol, V = {V} dm³ = {V}/1000 m³, T = {T} °C = {T} + 273 K, R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
solutionChain.justification: With R in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ the volume must be in m³ and the temperature in KELVIN. Converting both here is worth two marks on its own.
An absolute temperature is required — a gas law with °C in it is simply wrong (PH-U02).
Ideal gas equation pV = nRT, rearranged for pressure.

misconceptions.statement: Left the temperature in degrees Celsius.
misconceptions.feedback: Gas laws need kelvin: {T} °C = {T+273} K. Using {T} directly makes the pressure far too small — and the marker sees it in one glance.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: The question is written in °C, and °C is the temperature scale you use every day.

misconceptions.feedback: R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ is the SI value, so V must be in m³: {V} dm³ = {V/1000} m³. Your pressure is 1000 times too small.
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: dm³ is the volume unit chemistry uses everywhere else, including molarity.
